subject: business-studies
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: What is enterprise in a business context?
options: The skill of spotting an opportunity and taking the risk to act on it
questions.explain: Enterprise involves identifying a business opportunity and taking the risk of acting on it.

questions.q: A common business objective for a brand-new start-up is most likely to be:
questions.explain: Survival is a key short-term objective for new businesses, which often face high failure rates early on.

questions.q: Which statement about a sole trader is correct?
options: They have unlimited liability for business debts
questions.explain: A sole trader has unlimited liability, meaning personal assets are at risk if the business cannot pay its debts.

questions.q: What does 'limited liability' mean for the owners of a private limited company (Ltd)?
options: Owners are personally responsible for all business debts
Owners can lose only the amount they invested
The business has limited time to operate
questions.explain: Limited liability means shareholders can only lose the money they invested, not their personal assets.

questions.q: What is the main purpose of a business plan?
options: To set out the aims, strategy and finances of the business to guide it and attract investment
To guarantee the business will succeed
To replace the need for any finance
questions.explain: A business plan outlines aims, strategy and financial forecasts, helping to guide decisions and secure funding.

questions.q: A business in the public sector is one that is:
options: Always run to make maximum profit
Owned and run by the government
questions.explain: The public sector is owned and controlled by the government, usually to provide public services.

questions.q: Which is an advantage of being a sole trader compared with a private limited company?
options: Shares can be sold to raise large amounts of finance
The business is quick and simple to set up with full control kept by the owner
questions.explain: Sole traders are simple to set up and the owner keeps full control, though they have unlimited liability.

questions.q: What is the difference between a merger and a takeover?
options: A merger is two firms agreeing to join; a takeover is one firm buying control of another
A takeover is two firms agreeing to join as equals
They are exactly the same thing
A merger always fails; a takeover always succeeds
questions.explain: In a merger two firms agree to combine; in a takeover one firm gains control of another, sometimes against its wishes.

questions.q: Which type of business ownership is owned by its shareholders but cannot sell shares to the general public?
questions.explain: A private limited company (Ltd) is owned by shareholders but its shares cannot be sold to the public.

questions.q: Which factor is LEAST likely to influence where a business chooses to locate?
options: The favourite colour of the owner
Proximity to customers or the market
Nearness to raw materials or suppliers
questions.explain: Location decisions are driven by factors like market, labour and supplies, not personal preferences like a favourite colour.

questions.q: A key benefit of buying a franchise rather than starting from scratch is that:
options: The franchisee keeps all profit and pays nothing to the franchisor
The business uses an established brand and proven business model
The franchisee can ignore the franchisor's rules
There is no risk of failure at all
questions.explain: A franchisee trades under an established brand with a proven format, reducing some of the risk of a start-up.

questions.q: Inorganic (external) growth occurs when a business:
options: Opens an extra branch using its own profits
Sells more of its existing products
Merges with or takes over another business
questions.explain: Inorganic growth comes from merging with or taking over another firm, rather than expanding internally.

questions.q: Which of these is an example of a stakeholder in a business?
questions.explain: Stakeholders are any groups with an interest in the business, including employees, customers and suppliers.

questions.q: What is the main role of an entrepreneur when starting a business?
options: To work only as an employee for a larger firm
To take a risk by organising resources to set up a business
To guarantee the business will make a profit
questions.explain: An entrepreneur takes the risk of combining resources (land, labour, capital) to create a new business.

questions.q: Which statement best describes the 'dynamic nature' of business?
options: Businesses never change once set up
Markets and conditions constantly change, so businesses must adapt to survive
Profit always stays the same each year
All businesses must be public limited companies
questions.explain: The dynamic nature of business means conditions change constantly, so firms must adapt to survive and grow.

questions.q: For taking on risk, an entrepreneur's main potential reward is:
options: Profit and being their own boss
questions.explain: In return for risk, entrepreneurs can earn profit and gain independence, though success is not guaranteed.

questions.q: Which is a common reason why new businesses fail?
questions.explain: Running out of cash (poor cash-flow management) is one of the most common causes of business failure.

questions.q: In a partnership, profits are usually:
questions.explain: Partners typically share the profits (and losses) of the business according to their agreement.

questions.q: What is the key difference between a public limited company (plc) and a private limited company (Ltd)?
options: A plc can sell shares to the general public on the stock exchange
questions.explain: A plc can sell its shares to the public on the stock exchange, whereas an Ltd cannot.

questions.q: Why might rapid growth be a risk for a business?
options: It can stretch cash flow and management, causing problems if not controlled
Growth always lowers costs with no downside
Growth removes the need for planning
questions.explain: Growing too quickly can overstretch cash and management, so growth carries risk as well as reward.

questions.q: What is 'organic growth'?
options: Growth by taking over a competitor
Growth from within, such as by selling more products or opening new branches
Growth by merging with another firm
questions.explain: Organic (internal) growth comes from expanding the existing business rather than merging or taking over another.

questions.q: Which of the following are the three factors of production?
questions.explain: The factors of production are land, labour and capital (with enterprise often added as a fourth).
